title: The Failure Manual Buffett Loved — From The Man Who Built Coca-Cola
subtitle: Don Keough watched Coke compound at 27% per year for 16 years. Then he wrote a book telling you exactly how to blow it.
sections_used: The Commandments: Spotting Bad Management Before It Costs You
Where The Book Holds Up In 2026

He's famously selective about what he attaches his name to. So when a book on business failure lands with a Buffett foreword, that's not a marketing move \u2014 that's a signal."}]}, {"type": "heading", "attrs": {"level": 2}, "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "TL;DR"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "content": ["Don Keough, the President and COO of Coca-Cola during its greatest era, wrote ", {"type": "text", "text": "The Ten Commandments of Business Failure", "marks": [{"type": "italic"}]}, " as an inversion: a list of exactly what companies do to destroy themselves. Every commandment is written as advice ", {"type": "text", "text": "for", "marks": [{"type": "italic"}]}, " failure \u2014 \"quit taking risks,\" \"be inflexible,\" \"assume infallibility\" \u2014 forcing you to read it backwards and notice how often you're accidentally following the script. Clay Finck and David Fagan (a CPA and early TIP Mastermind member) work through the book's lessons for investors and business owners alike. Under Keough and Roberto Goizueta, Coke's stock compounded at 27% per annum from 1981 to 1997, excluding dividends. The man knew a thing or two about building something durable \u2014 and, crucially, about watching others throw it away."]}, {"type": "heading", "attrs": {"level": 2}, "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Core Thesis"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "The book's insight is deceptively simple: failure follows patterns. Not unique, tragic, hard-to-see patterns \u2014 obvious, repeatable ones. Keough watched great businesses collapse from the inside, and what struck him wasn't the complexity of the disasters. It was how predictable they were. Companies didn't fail because the market changed or competitors got lucky. They failed because the people at the top started doing identifiable, nameable things. Keough catalogued them."}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "The inversion frame is what makes this different from every other business book. Instead of \"here's how to win,\" it's \"here's precisely how to lose.\" Charlie Munger would approve. The goal isn't to tell you what to do \u2014 it's to burn into your memory the behaviors that guarantee ruin, so you'll recognize them when they start creeping in. Investors should read this not just for business strategy, but as a checklist for assessing management quality."}]}, {"type": "heading", "attrs": {"level": 2}, "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "The Commandments: Spotting Bad Management Before It Costs You"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "The episode hits several of Keough's commandments \u2014 and they map directly to what investors see in earnings calls, annual letters, and management interviews."}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Quit taking risks.", "marks": [{"type": "bold"}]}, " The best businesses are always hunting for the next thing. Complacency is the earliest sign of decay \u2014 when a company stops taking risks, management is usually protecting something (their bonus, their legacy, their stock price) rather than building something. Coca-Cola under Keough kept expanding, kept experimenting. Not always successfully \u2014 this is the same team behind New Coke \u2014 but always moving."]}, {"type": "paragraph", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Be inflexible.", "marks": [{"type": "bold"}]}, " \"Inflexibility is a recipe for failure.\" Fagan brings his own experience running a small accounting firm, watching rigid businesses get outmaneuvered by more adaptive competitors. For investors, this shows up in how management responds to disruption. Do they double down on the old model, or do they acknowledge the landscape has changed?"]}, {"type": "paragraph", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Assume infallibility.", "marks": [{"type": "bold"}]}, " \"Perception is everything and we shouldn't assume infallibility.\" This is the trap of past success. The company that hit a 10-year run starts believing it's immune. Keough saw this destroy businesses that had every reason to survive. The tell for investors: when management stops citing risks and starts writing annual letters that read like victory laps."]}, {"type": "paragraph", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Put all your faith in experts and outside consultants.", "marks": [{"type": "bold"}]}, " The best leaders balance outside expertise with internal intuition. The companies that fail often outsource their thinking \u2014 pile on consultants, hire external strategy firms, and stop trusting the people who actually know the business. It sounds like responsible governance. It's actually abdication."]}, {"type": "paragraph", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Pessimism as paralysis.", "marks": [{"type": "bold"}]}, " Keough's final emphasis \u2014 and Clay makes it central \u2014 is that optimism isn't naive. It's structurally necessary. \"Pessimism is paralyzing.\" The great operators maintain genuine conviction that the future is worth building toward. When that conviction disappears from a management team, you feel it in every investor call. Things get hedged, qualified, managed-down."]}, {"type": "heading", "attrs": {"level": 2}, "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Practical Applications For Investors"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Run the Keough checklist on your portfolio companies. Not the 10-Q. Not the analyst reports. The commandments."}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Does management still talk about what they're building, or only about protecting what they have? That's the risk-aversion commandment. Are they citing the same strategy from five years ago, unchanged, while the industry reshapes around them? Inflexibility. Have they stopped acknowledging anything that could go wrong? Infallibility."}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Buffett invested in Coca-Cola in 1988 \u2014 seven years into Keough's tenure. He knew Keough personally and wrote the book's foreword. That relationship and his assessment of management culture were part of the investment thesis, not just the brand moat. This book is Keough putting that management philosophy on paper. The 27% annual compounding was the output. The commandments (avoided) were the input."}]}, {"type": "heading", "attrs": {"level": 2}, "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Where The Book Holds Up In 2026"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "The commandments age well because they're about human nature, not industry dynamics. \"Be inflexible\" is as relevant to a software company resisting AI adoption as it was to a retailer refusing to acknowledge e-commerce. \"Assume infallibility\" describes plenty of recent boardrooms as clearly as any company Keough watched in the 1990s."}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "What the book can't cover \u2014 and what Fagan's conversation with Clay fills in \u2014 is the small business dimension. Keough's lens is Fortune 500. But every commandment scales down. The small firm that stops taking on new service lines, trusts the way they've always done things, assumes client relationships are permanent \u2014 they're running the same failure playbook as the boardrooms Keough watched implode. The patterns don't care about your revenue."}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "This is a short book. It's not a 400-page management treatise. Read it once and you'll start hearing Keough's commandments everywhere \u2014 in earnings calls, in startup postmortems, in the news cycles around companies that \"suddenly\" fell apart. The failure was never sudden."}]}, {"type": "horizontal_rule"}, {"type": "paragraph", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Books & resources mentioned:", "marks": [{"type": "bold"}]}]}, {"type": "bullet_list", "content": [{"type": "list_item", "content": [{"type": "paragraph", "content": ["Don Keough, ", {"type": "text", "text": "The Ten Commandments of Business Failure", "marks": [{"type": "italic"}]}]}]}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Original podcast: ", "marks": [{"type": "italic"}]}, {"type": "text", "text": "The Investor's Podcast Network", "marks": [{"type": "italic"}, {"type": "link", "attrs": {"href": "https://www.theinvestorspodcast.com/", "target": "_blank"}}]}, {"type": "text", "text": " \u2014 episode 639 (TIP639).", "marks": [{"type": "italic"}]}]}]}
